derivations.claim: Put $\tau=\chi u$, $\kappa=k/\chi$, $x_H=\chi U_H$, and $\lambda=Ak>0$. In the length coordinate $\tau$, the map $x(\tau):=\ell(\tau/\chi)$ satisfies $x(\tau)=x_H+\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)$, since $\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)=-\chi A e^{-\kappa\tau}$. By [F1], $U_\kappa$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,0)$; the positive affine map $y\mapsto x_H+\lambda y$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $(-\infty,0)$ onto $(-\infty,x_H)$. Since $u\mapsto\tau=\chi u$ is also a positive linear diffeomorphism, $\ell$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,\ell_H)$, with smooth inverse $u_\ell(x)=\chi^{-1}U_\kappa^{-1}((x-x_H)/\lambda)$. Differentiating the supplied coordinate formula gives $\ell'(u)=\chi\lambda e^{-\kappa\chi u}=\chi Ak e^{-ku}$ and hence $U'(u)=Ak e^{-ku}>0$. If $\operatorname{supp}g\subseteq[a,b]$, then $\operatorname{supp}f_g\subseteq[\ell(a),\ell(b)]\subset(-\infty,\ell_H)$, so the zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Thus $J(f_g)$ is defined by [F1]–[F2].

The map $(u,v)\mapsto(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ is a smooth diffeomorphism, so [F4] transports the two-variable test pairing with Jacobian $\ell'(u)\ell'(v)$. Since $\ell=\chi U$, the regularized identity $\chi^2[-(4\pi)^{-1}(\chi s-i\epsilon)^{-2}]=-(4\pi)^{-1}(s-i\epsilon/\chi)^{-2}$ shows that the positive unit scale cancels in the boundary distribution, giving the stated seconds-coordinate kernel. Positivity is the supplied Fock norm identity $W(g,g)=\|h_{f_g}\|_2^2\ge0$ from [F1].

On the finite-particle domain, the left vacuum annihilates every creation term and the right vacuum is annihilated by every annihilation operator. Commuting the annihilation part of the leftmost $J(f_{g_1})$ through the later fields, [F3] replaces each commutator by its scalar two-point contraction; the term with the annihilator reaching the right vacuum vanishes. Hence
$$M_n(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=\sum_{j=2}^n M_2(g_1,g_j)\,M_{n-2}(g_2,\ldots,\widehat{g_j},\ldots,g_n).$$
The base cases are $M_0=1$ and $M_1=0$. Induction gives zero for odd $n$ and the stated sum over pair partitions for even $n$.

derivations.claim:
Put $\tau=\chi u$, $x(\tau)=\chi U(\tau/\chi)$, and $\kappa=k/\chi$. Then
$$x(\tau)=\chi U_H+Ak\left(-\kappa^{-1}e^{-\kappa\tau}\right).$$
The coefficient $\lambda=Ak$ is positive. For $C_\epsilon(s)=-(4\pi)^{-1}(s-i\epsilon)^{-2}$, the exact identity $\lambda^2C_\epsilon(\lambda s)=C_{\epsilon/\lambda}(s)$ shows that a positive affine rescaling and translation leave the lower-boundary covariance unchanged. By [F1]–[F2], the canonical length-coordinate covariance is $C_\kappa$. Returning to seconds multiplies its kernel by $\chi^2$, so
$$C_k(s)=\chi^2C_\kappa(\chi s)=-\frac{k^2}{16\pi}\operatorname{csch}^2\left(\frac{k}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$

Fix $\omega$ and write $\Gamma=\Gamma(\omega)$, $\alpha=\sqrt{\Gamma}$, and $\beta=\sqrt{1-\Gamma}$. By [F11], $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$ are the unique nonnegative roots and $\alpha^2+\beta^2=\Gamma+(1-\Gamma)=1$. Hence the matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\Gamma}&\sqrt{1-\Gamma}\\-\sqrt{1-\Gamma}&\sqrt{\Gamma}\end{pmatrix}$$
is real orthogonal. The tensor-factor operators commute on $\mathscr D_{\rm fin}$; expanding their commutators and applying [F5] gives $[b,b^\dagger]=[d,d^\dagger]=I$ and $[b,d^\dagger]=[b,d]=0$ on that core. Since $\Psi_\omega\in D$, the operator $b\Psi_\omega$ is defined, and
$$b\Psi_\omega=\alpha(a_{\mathbb C}(1)\psi_\omega)\otimes\Omega_e+\beta\,\psi_\omega\otimes(e\Omega_e).$$
The environment term vanishes because $e\Omega_e=0$. Therefore $\mathfrak n_{\rm out}(\omega)=\|b\Psi_\omega\|^2=\alpha^2\|a_{\mathbb C}(1)\psi_\omega\|^2=\Gamma n_\omega$, by the quadratic-form definition in the Statement.

In [F3] take $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$ and $b=\kappa/2$. For the seconds-frequency variable, Fourier change of variables gives $S_k(\omega)=\chi S_\kappa(\omega/\chi)$, hence $S_k(\omega)=\omega/[2(e^{2\pi\omega/k}-1)]$ away from zero and $S_k(0)=\chi\kappa/(4\pi)=k/(4\pi)$. Substitution of $-\omega$ and cancellation of the common factor gives $S_k(-\omega)=e^{2\pi\omega/k}S_k(\omega)$ for $\omega>0$.

Put $x=\theta\omega>0$. By the mean-value theorem [F9] on $[0,x]$, for some $c\in(0,x)$, $\exp(x)-\exp(0)=x\exp'(c)=x\exp(c)>0$, using [F8] and [F7]; [F6] gives $\exp(0)=1$. Hence $n_\theta(\omega)>0$ and $0<\Gamma_*(\omega)<1$. If any filter has $\Gamma(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=n_\theta(\omega)$ at every positive frequency, division by this positive value gives $\Gamma(\omega)=1$ everywhere, so no nonconstant filter preserves the same width. If $0<\omega_1<\omega_2$, applying [F9] on $[\theta\omega_1,\theta\omega_2]$ gives $\exp(\theta\omega_2)-\exp(\theta\omega_1)=\theta(\omega_2-\omega_1)\exp'(c)>0$ for some intermediate $c$, by [F8] and [F7]. Thus $\Gamma_*$ is nonconstant. By [F10], $\exp(2x)-1=(\exp(x)-1)(\exp(x)+1)$; therefore $\Gamma_*(\omega)n_\theta(\omega)=1/(\exp(2x)-1)=n_{2\theta}(\omega)$. The varying filter can thus produce a Planck occupation at a different width.
